title: Fully alive
hookLine: Irenaeus: the glory of God is a human being fully alive
carry: awake, creative, glad to be in a body

lines: HE SAW POLYCARP IN HIS YOUTH.
ONE SHORT LINE IN THE MIDDLE.
cards: A few days ago we met Polycarp, the old bishop who wouldn't curse Christ. A man named Irenaeus writes that he saw Polycarp in his own early youth, and remembers him.

Irenaeus grows up to be a bishop himself, and writes a long, careful book against teachings he believes are pulling Christians away from the faith they received. It's big and argumentative, full of names and systems.
And somewhere in the middle sits one short line that people still quote today.

teach.b: In its old Latin text, the line reads gloria Dei vivens homo. Word for word: the glory of God, a living human being. Some modern versions say: the glory of God is a human being fully alive.
Fully alive is a translator's way of bringing out vivens, living; they aren't separate words in the Latin. And the sentence goes on.

teach.h: AND THE LIFE OF HUMANS: SEEING GOD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. So it's a circle. God is glorified when people are truly alive, and people are truly alive when they see God.

teach.h: THE BODY IS NOT A MISTAKE.
teach.b: Some teachers in Irenaeus's world taught that the physical world was a mistake, that the body was a prison, and that real spiritual life meant escaping it. Irenaeus pushes back hard.
The one God made the world, and made it good. God works with dust and breath, and the Son of God took on flesh.

It's the note the Bible strikes in its first chapter: "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." For Irenaeus, being human isn't a problem to be solved. It's what God is bringing to life.
Christians hear the line in different ways. Some hear joy: God delights in people who are awake, creative, glad to be in a body.
Others quickly add the second half, so fully alive never just means busy or thrilled; for Irenaeus, the deepest life is seeing God.
Both halves belong to the one sentence.

how: Some Christians quote Irenaeus's line in sermons, retreats and books about prayer and creativity, and some pair it with its second half, that the life of a human being is the vision of God.

o: always busy and thrilled, never resting at all
a human being truly living, God's glory, says Irenaeus
living a long life with no illness or pain

p: the life of humans is seeing God
Irenaeus saw him in his youth

s: the words fully alive are written out separately in the Latin
the Latin says vivens homo, a living human being. fully alive brings out its force.
Irenaeus's sentence has a second half
and the life of a human being is the vision of God.
Irenaeus taught that the body is a prison to escape
that's what he argued against. he says the one God made the world, and made it good.

games.q: you're Irenaeus. some teachers say the body is a prison and the world a mistake. what do you write?
o: agree: the spirit must escape the flesh.
the glory of God is a living human being.
leave it alone: it's not worth an argument.
games.why: he writes a long book of arguments, and in it: the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of a human being is seeing God.

practice: Notice that you're in a body: feet, hands, the weight of you in the chair.
Then let your mind go to something that makes you more yourself, not just busy, like cooking for people, walking under trees, singing badly or fixing a thing.
If you pray, offer it to God as a thank you; if you don't, just hold it, and look forward to it.

wordCard.voice: Fully alive. From Irenaeus: the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of a human being is the vision of God.

orig.note: Latin: the glory of God, a living human being. the old Latin text of Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.20.7.
